findings.title: Backup named 'nightly' is type ON_DEMAND - it runs once at apply, never nightly
findings.explanation: The resource label, the backup_id suffix (cluster_id + '-nightly') and the output all present this as a recurring nightly backup, but type = "ON_DEMAND" produces a single point-in-time backup at apply and never repeats. AlloyDB's AUTOMATED and CONTINUOUS backup types are set by the service, not by this resource, so this block can never become a schedule. No rule fires because ON_DEMAND is a perfectly valid value - the mismatch exists only between the name and the semantics. Real nightly coverage already comes from google_alloydb_cluster.main's automated_backup_policy (daily 02:00 weekly_schedule), so the risk is an operator believing this resource is the nightly job and relaxing the cluster policy.
findings.remediation: Either drop this resource (the cluster's automated_backup_policy already provides daily backups plus a 14-day continuous window), or rename it to what it actually is - resource "google_alloydb_backup" "initial" with backup_id = "${var.cluster_id}-initial" - and document it as a one-shot seed backup.

findings.title: pgAudit is switched on but no pgaudit.log classes are set, so no audit records are emitted
findings.explanation: database_flags sets alloydb.enable_pgaudit = "on", which only makes the pgaudit extension available - it does not itself log anything. pgAudit emits records only once pgaudit.log names one or more statement classes (ddl, write, role, ...); with that flag unset the default is 'none' and the instance produces no audit trail while appearing audited. Rules miss this because the one attribute they would check is present and correct - the gap is the missing companion key in the same map. Blast radius is the whole database: no record of DDL, privilege changes or writes for forensics or compliance.
findings.remediation: Add the companion flag to database_flags: "pgaudit.log" = "ddl,role,write". The map is also hard-coded with no variable, so consumers cannot tune the classes - consider merge()-ing a var.database_flags override at the same time. The pgaudit extension must additionally be CREATEd in each database for logging to start.

findings.title: Example creates the AlloyDB service identity and cluster without ever enabling alloydb.googleapis.com
findings.explanation: google_project_service_identity calls services.generateServiceIdentity, which fails when the service is not already enabled on the project, and the module's cluster and instance need the API too - but example/examplea contains no google_project_service for alloydb.googleapis.com (nor for servicenetworking.googleapis.com or cloudkms.googleapis.com). No rule fires because each resource is individually valid; the defect is a missing prerequisite in the composition. On a fresh project this example fails on first apply, and since module.alloydb depends_on the KMS IAM member which depends on this identity, the whole chain stalls. This is an apply-time correctness issue, so 'reliability' is a best-fit principle rather than a precise one.
findings.remediation: Add example/examplea/google_project_service.alloydb.tf enabling alloydb.googleapis.com, servicenetworking.googleapis.com and cloudkms.googleapis.com with disable_on_destroy = false, and add depends_on = [google_project_service.alloydb] to google_project_service_identity.alloydb.

findings.title: Service networking connection has no deletion_policy, so destroying the example hangs or orphans the peering
findings.explanation: Deleting a servicenetworking connection while a producer resource (here the AlloyDB cluster) still holds addresses in the peered range is a well-known GCP failure mode: the delete call errors or blocks, then takes google_compute_global_address.alloydb and google_compute_network.alloydb down with it. The provider exposes deletion_policy = "ABANDON" precisely for this and it is unset. coverage_by_type has no entry for google_service_networking_connection at all, so no deterministic rule looks at it. Destroy-time correctness rather than a security gap, so 'reliability' is a best-fit principle.
findings.remediation: Add deletion_policy = "ABANDON" to google_service_networking_connection.alloydb so destroying the example abandons the peering instead of failing mid-destroy.

findings.title: var.kms_key_name is marked sensitive though a KMS key resource name is not a secret
findings.explanation: kms_key_name carries a resource path (projects/.../cryptoKeys/...), which is an identifier, not key material - it is visible in the console and in every audit log line. Marking it sensitive redacts it from plan output in all four encryption_config blocks, making it impossible to review at plan time which key is being applied or to spot a CMEK change, and it forces sensitivity to propagate to anything derived from it. This is the inverse of the secret-detection blind spot: a reference to a key treated as the key itself.
findings.remediation: Remove `sensitive = true` from variable "kms_key_name" in variables.tf line 45; keep the description and the non-empty validation unchanged.

suggested_policies.rationale: AlloyDB has no audit-logging policy at all - coverage_by_type lists only HLD_GCP_395 (backup CMEK), HLD_GCP_323/325/352/353/354 (cluster) and HLD_GCP_351 (instance public IP). holden already ships the exact analogue for Cloud SQL (HLD_GCP_219, 'Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instances must enable pgAudit extension', logging-and-monitoring/MEDIUM), so the same control for AlloyDB is a straight coverage gap. The check is a pure attribute check on two well-known keys of google_alloydb_instance.database_flags, fires identically on any Terraform using the type, and catches both halves of HOLDEN_AI_002 - the extension being off, and the extension being on with no log classes selected (the state this module is in).
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_527
name: AlloyDB instances must enable pgAudit and select audit log classes
principle: logging-and-monitoring
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  AlloyDB emits database audit records only when the pgAudit extension is
  enabled via the alloydb.enable_pgaudit database flag AND pgaudit.log names
  one or more statement classes. Enabling the extension alone leaves the
  default of 'none', so the instance produces no audit trail while appearing
  to be audited, leaving no record of DDL, privilege changes or data writes
  for forensics or compliance.
remediation: |
  ```hcl
  resource "google_alloydb_instance" "primary" {
    instance_type = "PRIMARY"

    database_flags = {
      "alloydb.enable_pgaudit" = "on"
      "pgaudit.log"            = "ddl,role,write"
    }
  }
  ```
  The pgaudit extension must also be created in each database
  (CREATE EXTENSION pgaudit;) for logging to begin.
resources:
  google_alloydb_instance:
    all:
      - path: 'database_flags["alloydb.enable_pgaudit"]'
        equals: "on"
      - path: 'database_flags["pgaudit.log"]'
        not_null: true
suggested_policies.dsl_extension_note: The path resolver is dot-separated only, so a map key that itself contains a dot cannot be addressed. Verified empirically in this repo: a policy with `path: database_flags.alloydb.enable_pgaudit` on google_alloydb_instance returned UNKNOWN with violation.attr_path 'database_flags.alloydb.enable_pgaudit' and actual: null, even though the resource sets database_flags = { "alloydb.enable_pgaudit" = "on" } - the resolver walked into a nonexistent map key 'alloydb'. Extension needed: support a bracketed, quoted literal segment in path, e.g. database_flags["alloydb.enable_pgaudit"], handled in the path splitter (wherever internal/policy splits the path on '.') so a segment enclosed in ["..."] is taken verbatim as one map key instead of being split on its dots. All other semantics unchanged - an absent key behaves exactly as an absent dotted attribute does today. This also unblocks Cloud SQL-style flag maps and any provider keying a map by a dotted namespace. Mirror the change in the path property description in schemas/policy.schema.json.
